newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker on rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker on rate hike fears.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened weaker on Thursday as concern about a near-term Bank of Canada rate hike weighed on prices and kept accounts away from the market, dealers said.

"Right now there's a bit of paranoia setting in, concern the central bank here might raise rates again," said one T-bill dealer with a bank-owned brokerage. "The accounts are not buying. They're not spending their money in the term."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.28 percent from 3.25 percent at the close of trading on Wednesday.

Dealers said there is nothing specific pointing to a near-term Bank of Canada rate hike, but cite signs of recent strength in the economy. Last month the Bank of Canada hiked interest rates by 25 basis points, its first such move in more than two years.
Accounts have avoided the market this morning because of rate hike fears, dealers said.

"Some people have been functioning on the expectation of the Bank of Canada raising rates today, so people have been paying up on the overnight," said one dealer with a Canadian bank. "There's very, very slow distribution."

The Canadian consumer price index report for June out this morning had no major impact on the money market, dealers said. The report showed the so-called core CPI rose 0.2 percent on the month and 2.0 percent on the year.

In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.59 percent from a 3.58 percent at the close of trading on Wednesday. The one-year T-bill softened to yield 4.08 percent from 4.06 percent.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.40 percent, in the upper half of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range.
